units: a neighbour recounts a night of observing
the instrument was set up on a balcony late in the evening
she first took a blurred streak for a plane
the sky then cleared
she recognised the comet that had been announced
she woke her brother, who grumbled before joining her
she noticed the object shifting between two glances
she plans to go again the next night, better equipped
text: My neighbour was still laughing about her night at the eyepiece when she told me the whole of it. She had set the instrument up on her balcony late in the evening, once the light had drained out of the sky. At first, she said, she could make out nothing but a smear of brightness, which she put down to a passing plane. Then the cloud broke up, and she saw where she had gone wrong: the pale streak she had been squinting at for half an hour was the comet everyone had been talking about. She woke her brother, who grumbled at being hauled out of bed and came out in his slippers all the same. Between one look and the next, she noticed, the thing had shifted along. She means to go up again the following night, with a flask and a blanket, having shivered for hours without once noticing.

units: glassmakers learned to polish even surfaces
the first instruments stopped distorting the images
stars until then invisible became observable
observers moved from description to measurement
star catalogues grew richer and more reliable
blurred patches turned out to be groups of stars
steadier mounts had to be built
a craft of precision mechanics was born of that need
text: Better lenses reshaped the study of the sky far beyond anything their makers had in mind. Once glassmakers worked out how to polish a surface evenly, the earliest instruments stopped bending what they showed, and stars nobody had ever seen came within reach. That sharpness had a further effect: observers gave up describing what they remembered and began measuring what lay in front of them. Catalogues grew thicker and steadier, and faint patches long taken for smears turned out to be crowds of separate stars. Mounts had to be rebuilt as well, since a trembling tube threw away everything the glass had gained. Out of that need came a whole craft of precision mechanics, with its worm screws, its gearing and its counterweights. Step by step, the glassmaker's bench changed the way the night sky was questioned.

units: a diffuse brightness hides the stars above built-up areas
the cause is the beam of lamps aimed upward
particles held in the air scatter that beam
faint stars become impossible to pick out
observers have to travel away from towns
tilting the lamps towards the ground and hooding them solves the problem
places that have applied this measure see their galaxy again
the measure also helps sleep, birds and spending
text: A milky glow now sits over every built-up area, and the stars behind it go out one by one. The trouble starts with lamps that throw part of their beam upward, where dust and damp air scatter it in every direction. A dome of brightness gathers above the rooftops, and the weaker stars simply drown in it. Anyone after a dark sky has to drive further and further out to find one. The cure costs next to nothing: tilt the fittings towards the ground and hood them so that no light escapes above the horizontal. Towns that have done so watch the pale band of our own galaxy come back over their squares. Residents sleep less fitfully, migrating birds find their bearings again, and the lighting bill drops. A dark sky has not been lost for good; it is waiting for someone to reach for the switch.

units: a stock farmer brings in a dark stone found on his land
a specialist compares it with an already authenticated sample
the two blocks look alike from the outside
cutting them open reveals differences inside
the authenticated sample holds frozen droplets and metal
the farmer's stone holds only stretched cavities
it comes in fact from foundry waste
magnetic pull explains the usual confusion
analysis of the metal content settled the question
text: A stock farmer carried a black stone into the laboratory, picked up in one of his fields and, he was certain, fallen out of the sky. The technician set it beside a reference sample, a meteorite recovered from a desert and catalogued long before. The two might have been twins: dark crust, surprising heft for their size, edges worn smooth. Cutting them open pulled their histories apart. The reference piece showed tiny frozen droplets, the beads found throughout the oldest rock, along with a bright metallic web that came up under polishing. The stone from the field held nothing but stretched bubbles, the mark of foundry slag cooled far too quickly. A magnet clung to both, which is why finders are so regularly misled. Only the ratio between two neighbouring metals settled it, and the farmer went home with an old lump of industrial waste.

units: preparing a session follows a settled order
power and backup lighting come first
a red torch keeps night vision from being spoiled
the optics must be aligned and cleaned before dark
the finder is set on a distant target while it is still light
the mount must stand on firm ground
the axis of the mount must point at the pole star
the observer should plan for clothing and a hot drink
the charts are gathered last of all
text: Getting ready for a night at the eyepiece works best in a settled order. Power comes first: a charged battery, cables coiled, a red torch so that notes can be read without wrecking your night vision. Optics next: the mirror aligned, the eyepieces wiped with a proper cloth, the finder trained on some distant landmark while there is still daylight to do it by. Then the mount, legs spread wide on firm ground, its axis swung round until it points at the pole star, so that tracking stays smooth for hours. Comfort deserves the same care: layers of clothing, a hot drink, a seat you can adjust, because sitting still chills you faster than you would think. Last of all, gather the paperwork, sky chart, target list, notebook and pencil. A wasted night rarely comes down to the kit; it comes down to something forgotten in the rush out of the door.

units: the craft left its parking orbit on instruction from the ground
short burns corrected a sideways drift
the pictures sent back showed at first a grey cratered plain
the ground proved rougher than expected
the original landing site was given up during the descent
sharp-edged boulders lay across the planned zone
a faint signal confirmed contact with the ground
dust thrown up by the thrusters settled without a cloud
drilling is announced after a recharging phase
text: The probe left its parking orbit shortly before dawn, on instructions sent up from the control room. All the way down its thrusters fired in short bursts, trimming out a sideways drift that had been spotted the day before. The pictures relayed home showed a grey plain pitted with shallow craters, and then ground a good deal rougher than anyone had allowed for. Halfway through the descent the team gave up on the site they had chosen, since sharp-edged boulders were sitting right across it. Contact was confirmed by a faint signal, arriving with the usual travel delay, to applause in the room. A side camera then caught the dust thrown up by the nozzle, which settled straight back without hanging in the air. Drilling, the mission leads said, would begin after a rest period, the lander having to charge its batteries in the sunlight first.

units: the crew spend their breaks at the observation window
the planet looks blue and streaked with white
the speed of the craft brings sunset round again and again
the lack of gravity sets loose objects floating
every piece of kit has to be fixed down or strapped
water pulling back leaves sandbanks in view
the glazing is thick and built up in several layers
a speck of grit at that speed would pierce an ordinary wall
passing into shadow brings condensation
text: Put your face to the window and you see at once why the crew spend every break here. Below, a blue marble streaked with white slides past, near enough that you can pick out the bends of the rivers. The craft moves so fast that dusk keeps coming round again: the sky catches fire, goes out, and catches fire once more. Inside, nothing ever drops. Weightlessness sends pens drifting up to the ceiling, so every tool has to be strapped down or held by a magnet. Along one coast a paler fringe shows through, because the water has pulled back off the sandbanks there. The glazing is thick, built up in layers, since a speck of grit travelling at that speed would go clean through an ordinary wall. When the station swings into shadow the pane mists over, and you wait for the warmth to come round again.

units: low orbit is filling with dead craft and fragments
each fragment travels fast enough to pierce a hull
each collision breeds fresh fragments
some altitudes risk becoming unusable
the lack of a binding rule keeps everyone idle
every craft ought to carry the means to leave its orbit at the end of its life
a passive tracking device would make avoidance more reliable
recovery vehicles ought to capture the heaviest wrecks
the cost of these measures is small against the loss of access
text: Must we wait for a serious collision before anything is done? Low orbit is filling up with wreckage: spent rocket stages, dead satellites, splinters left behind by destructive tests. Every one of those shards moves fast enough to punch through a hull, and every impact breeds fresh shards, which puts whole bands of altitude at risk of becoming unusable. Operators pass the blame round between them, no binding rule obliging any of them to act. Three steps would turn this round. Require, first, that every craft carry enough propellant to drop itself out of orbit once its work is over. Impose, second, a passive tracking device, so that avoidance manoeuvres stop resting on guesswork. Fund, third, tugs able to grapple the heaviest hulks. The bill looks steep until you set it against the loss of an access our networks take for granted.

units: a cataloguer of nebulae worked from a desk
her colleagues observed directly under the dome
cloud often cut their sessions short
she examined photographic plates through a magnifier
she measured the spread and the shade of pale patches
her colleagues offered impressions, she offered measurements
a single plate took up a whole session
one scratch was enough to spoil the examination
she told two kinds of diffuse object apart
those who came after inherited her classification
text: The woman who kept the register of nebulae hardly ever left her desk, and it was from there that she saw further than the colleagues posted under the dome. They watched on perhaps one night in two, and cloud shut them down more often than not. She sat over photographic plates instead, holding pale smudges side by side, measuring how far they spread, noting their shade through a magnifier. Where the others wrote down an impression, she wrote down a figure. Her patience was that of a needleworker: one plate swallowed a whole session, and a single scratch across the glass could ruin the lot. In the end she sorted the fuzzy objects into two families, the one woven out of gas, the other made of stars beyond counting. Those who came after inherited a classification that no run of nights under the dome would have produced.

units: the instrument tested belongs to the cheapest range
the mirror gives sharp stars right to the edge of the field
the mount lacks weight and shakes at the slightest touch
every focusing move sets off a wobble to be waited out
the eyepiece supplied gives a narrow field and a soft image
the diagonal throws unwanted reflections
the finder adjusts without tools and holds its alignment
the manual says nothing about adjusting the mirrors
the verdict advises replacing the mount first
text: The budget instrument we put through its paces deserves judging part by part, with no allowances made. The optics first: the main mirror has an honest figure to it, and stars stay as points right out to the edge of the field, which is more than the price would lead you to expect. The mount next, far too light, shuddering at a touch, so that every twist of the focuser sets off a wobble you must simply wait out. The accessories disappoint. The eyepiece in the box gives a cramped field and a soft image, while the diagonal throws stray reflections across bright stars. The finder, to be fair, adjusts by hand and holds its alignment from one night to the next. Then the manual, hurried in the writing and silent on adjusting the mirrors, which the buyer will be facing inside a week. Verdict: a decent tube on a mount not up to carrying it.
